paragraphs.en: Your collection holds the 80 groszy Frombork stamp of 1960, engraved in violet-blue. A square brick tower with a pyramid roof stands at the left. paragraphs.en: Matejko painted "Astronomer Copernicus, or Conversations with God" in 1873, 400 years after Copernicus was born. At night, Copernicus kneels on the high balcony of a tower, with the spires of Frombork cathedral behind him. The long wooden instrument at his back forms a cross against the sky.

paragraphs.en: The Copernicus museum in Frombork writes that he kept his books and manuscripts in the tower and stayed there himself in dangerous times, because its walls could be defended. He observed the sky from the garden of his canonry, his main house. There he set up instruments of fir wood on a well-levelled slab.

paragraphs.en: A stroke in December 1542 left Copernicus unable to speak. The book came out in 1543. Copernicus died in Frombork that year, probably on 21 May. Bishop Tiedemann Giese wrote to Rheticus that Copernicus saw the finished book only at the last moment, on the day he died. The Copernicus portal of the university in Toruń thinks it more likely that the book reached Frombork after his death.

paragraphs.en: In July 1626, during the Thirty Years' War, Frombork surrendered to King Gustav II Adolf of Sweden. His troops took the chapter library to Stockholm, with the books Copernicus had owned. The king later gave them to the university library in Uppsala.
